input: I'm a hobbyist with one GPU. What's still hard about teaching a robot arm a new task from just a few demonstrations?
verdict: Same robot arm question with the wider search. 80 papers, 79 in full, 191 of 203 quotes kept (94%), 35 s. Six problems, all on the question, every first step names a real paper from the run. Weakness: each problem comes from one group, so none shows independent labs agreeing, and one (generalization to complex real-world settings) is generic. Was the second example until the eleventh run replaced it.
search: Searching arXiv for “one-shot imitation learning manipulation”, “meta-imitation learning few demonstrations”, “few-shot imitation learning”, “one-shot imitation learning”, “meta-imitation learning”

terms.meaning: teaching a robot to perform a new task using only a small number of example demonstrations
learning a new task from a single demonstration by the human teacher

sentences.text: These papers show that few-demonstration robot learning still struggles with compounding errors over long horizons, sharp performance drops as demonstrations decrease, sensitivity to distribution shifts like new object poses or lighting, and the need for safe exploration during real-world trial-and-error.
A single demonstration must transfer across viewpoint, grasp, and object changes while rejecting disturbances during execution, which requires both trajectory transfer and closed-loop stability.
Demonstration data itself is often noisy and temporally irregular, and standard downsampling cannot fix speed-induced non-uniformity or redundant pauses that degrade policy learning.

Richer supervision signals like language critiques or recoverability-conditioned exploration help, but current methods still trade off between conservative safety and sufficient coverage of recovery regions near expert behavior.

problems.title: Tracking fails under occlusion, motion blur, or poor surface properties

statements.quote: execution requires the functional-part points to remain trackable; large motions outside the camera views, severe occlusion, or unreliable depth on transparent or specular surfaces can break tracking.
statements.label: tracking fails under occlusion, motion blur, or poor surface properties

problems.explanation: Tracking breaks when objects are hidden, move too fast, or have tricky surfaces like glass or shiny metal. The robot loses the points it uses to know where things are. Solving this would let robots keep working even when the view gets messy.
problems.first_step: Run the code from "POIL: Point-based One-Shot Imitation Learning with Stable Dynamical Systems" on a scene with a transparent or specular object and watch where tracking fails.

problems.title: Recovery fails under diverse failure modes due to reliance on single-trajectory data

statements.quote: for tasks with highly diverse failure modes, AutoSERL’s recovery mechanism cannot recover from failures effectively during training because it relies on information from only a single trajectory.
statements.label: Recovery fails under diverse failure modes due to reliance on single-trajectory data

problems.explanation: The robot can't recover from different kinds of mistakes because it only learns from one successful demonstration. Real tasks have many ways to go wrong. Fixing this would make robots more resilient in practice.
problems.first_step: Run the AutoSERL code from "One Demonstration Is Enough for Real-World Robotic Reinforcement Learning" on a task where the robot can fail in several ways, dropping, slipping, misaligning, and log where recovery breaks down.

problems.title: Generalization to complex real-world robotics

statements.quote: it remains an open question how well the approach generalizes to more complex and dynamic real-world robotic settings.
statements.label: generalization to complex real-world robotics

problems.explanation: We don't know if the method works on real robots with noise, distractions, and unexpected changes. Lab results often don't transfer. Answering this would show whether the approach is ready for deployment.
problems.first_step: Take the code from "Language-Critique Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations" and test it on a real robot arm with a slightly different task than the paper used.

problems.title: Extension to visuomotor policies not yet achieved

statements.quote: We plan to extend this work to visuomotor policies using pretrained representations and lightweight learning methods.
statements.label: extension to visuomotor policies not yet achieved

problems.explanation: The current method doesn't use camera input directly for control. Adding vision would let the robot react to what it sees instead of relying on fixed representations. This is a key step toward general visuomotor skills.
problems.first_step: Take the code from "Training-Free Imitation Learning with Closed-Form Diffusion Policies" and add a pretrained visual encoder like ResNet to feed images into the policy.

problems.title: Predicate vocabulary and rules require manual design per domain

statements.quote: Our predicate vocabulary and rules are currently hand-crafted per domain; learning them via predicate-invention methods [[38](#bib.bib46)] is an immediate next step.
statements.label: Predicate vocabulary and rules require manual design per domain

problems.explanation: Right now humans must write the logic rules for each new task by hand. Automating this would let robots learn new domains without expert engineering each time. It's the difference between programming and learning.
problems.first_step: Run the code from "Neurosymbolic Imitation Learning with Human Guidance: A Privileged Information Approach" on a simple domain, then try replacing one hand-crafted predicate with a learned classifier.

problems.title: Uncertainty and recoverability estimation remains unreliable far from data

statements.quote: Future work may improve the two signals underlying acquisition by developing better calibrated epistemic uncertainty estimates and more reliable recoverability estimates beyond finite-horizon world-model imagination and discriminator scores, especially farther from current data support.
statements.label: uncertainty and recoverability estimation remains unreliable far from data

problems.explanation: The robot's confidence and recovery predictions get unreliable in unfamiliar states. Better estimates would let it explore safely instead of freezing or crashing. This matters for any robot that must go beyond its training data.
problems.first_step: Run the code from "Beyond Conservatism: Recoverability-Conditioned Exploration for Model-Based Imitation Learning" and measure how uncertainty and recoverability scores change as the robot moves farther from training states.
